prompt_free_text:
This paper presents Agent S, an open framework for desktop GUI automation with multimodal language models. The core proposal combines three ingredients: hierarchical manager-worker planning, retrieval from both external web knowledge and internal memories, and an Agent-Computer Interface that exposes a language-centric, bounded action space grounded through an accessibility tree augmented with OCR. Empirically, the paper reports a substantial improvement over the OSWorld baseline and additional gains on WindowsAgentArena without explicit adaptation. Overall, I found the paper timely, practically relevant, and reasonably well engineered. The problem setting is important, the benchmark choice is appropriate, and the reported gains are large enough to merit attention. At the same time, several aspects of the work are more systems-integration than fundamentally new algorithmic contributions, and some methodological details and evaluation choices leave open questions about fairness, reproducibility, and the exact source of the gains.

The strongest aspect of the paper is that it tackles a genuinely difficult and increasingly important setting: open-ended computer use through GUI interaction. The paper identifies three real bottlenecks in current agents—domain knowledge, long-horizon planning, and grounding in dynamic interfaces—and the proposed architecture is well aligned with these challenges. The manager/worker decomposition is intuitive, and the distinction between narrative memory for high-level task summaries and episodic memory for subtask-level execution traces is sensible. The ACI component is also a meaningful practical contribution: using accessibility trees plus OCR to create a more language-friendly observation space, and constraining actions to a small set of primitives, is a good design choice for current MLLM agents. The empirical improvements on OSWorld are nontrivial: moving from 11.21% to 20.58% overall success is a large absolute gain in this difficult benchmark, and the category-wise improvements in Daily and Professional tasks are especially notable.

I also appreciate that the paper goes beyond a single headline number. The ablations attempt to isolate the effects of web knowledge, narrative memory, episodic memory, hierarchical planning, and ACI. The error analysis is useful and, importantly, honest: even with the proposed framework, execution and grounding remain major failure modes. The cross-benchmark evaluation on WindowsAgentArena is another positive sign, since many agent papers overfit to one environment or one benchmark’s interface conventions.

That said, the paper’s novelty should be characterized carefully. Most of the ingredients have clear precedents: hierarchical planning, retrieval-augmented prompting, verbal memory/reflection, accessibility-tree grounding, OCR augmentation, and constrained action spaces have all appeared in adjacent agent literature. The contribution here is primarily in the integration and adaptation of these ideas to desktop GUI control, rather than in a sharply new learning or planning algorithm. That is not necessarily a problem for a systems-oriented contribution, but the paper occasionally overstates novelty. For example, “experience-augmented hierarchical planning” is a reasonable label for the combination, but the paper does not establish a fundamentally new planning formalism; it is closer to a retrieval-augmented manager-worker prompting pipeline with memory updates. Similarly, the ACI extension to GUI agents is useful, but it is more an adaptation of existing ACI ideas than a wholly new interface paradigm.

A more serious concern is evaluation rigor and fairness. The paper compares against OSWorld baselines, but Agent S appears to benefit from several additional components beyond the baseline: online web search, OCR-augmented accessibility trees, memory built from self-supervised exploration, and a different action abstraction. This makes the comparison somewhat bundled. The ablations help, but they are conducted on a 65-task subset rather than the full benchmark, and some key comparisons are not fully controlled. For instance, it would be important to know how much of the gain comes from the ACI alone under exactly matched model, prompt budget, and observation budget; how much comes from web retrieval alone; and how much comes from memory accumulated from benchmark-adjacent exploration tasks. The paper does include some of this qualitatively, but the evidence is not yet as clean as it could be.

Relatedly, the memory construction procedure raises possible contamination concerns. The initial memory is built from “top 50 most common tasks” from applications used in OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena, plus environment-aware tasks generated from initial benchmark environments. Even if these are not identical to test tasks, they are benchmark-adjacent and may encode substantial prior knowledge about the same apps, layouts, and workflows. This is not necessarily invalid, especially if the goal is continual open-world learning, but it does complicate the interpretation of “zero-shot” or generalization claims. The paper should be much more explicit about whether any exploration tasks are derived from the same applications, websites, or initial states as evaluation tasks; whether there is any overlap in task templates or latent workflows; and whether memory is frozen before evaluation or updated online during test-time across benchmark tasks. If memory is updated continually during evaluation, then task ordering matters and the reported numbers may reflect a form of benchmark-specific adaptation. This is a central issue and deserves much clearer treatment.

The use of online web search is another point that needs clarification. On one hand, it is a realistic and valuable capability for agents. On the other hand, it changes the problem definition relative to baselines that may not use external search. If the benchmark is intended to measure pure in-environment competence, web retrieval may provide an additional information channel that is not equally available to all methods. The paper should therefore report separate numbers with and without web access on the full benchmark, not only on the ablation subset, and discuss latency/cost implications. It would also help to characterize failure cases where web knowledge is misleading or stale.

The paper’s methodological description is generally understandable, but several details are underspecified. The retrieval setup needs more precision: how large are the narrative and episodic memories at evaluation time, what similarity metric and top-k are used, how are summaries formatted, how are conflicting retrieved experiences handled, and how often does retrieval return irrelevant memories? The self-evaluator is especially important but somewhat vague. Since it determines what gets stored, its precision matters greatly. How accurate is it at labeling successful subtasks and summarizing useful strategies? The paper claims that summarized trajectories outperform raw trajectories, but the mechanism is not deeply analyzed. A more direct evaluation of memory quality would strengthen the work.

I also found the statistical treatment limited. The main results are single success-rate numbers without confidence intervals or repeated runs. Given the stochasticity of MLLM agents and the sensitivity to prompting, retrieval, and environment timing, some estimate of variance would be valuable. This is especially true for the ablation subset of 65 tasks, where differences of a few points may not be stable. Even if full repeated evaluation is expensive, bootstrapped confidence intervals over tasks or repeated runs on a smaller subset would improve credibility.

Another weakness is that efficiency is largely ignored. The paper acknowledges this in the conclusion, but it remains a practical concern because the proposed system adds multiple expensive components: web search, two-stage retrieval, hierarchical replanning, OCR, and self-evaluation. In GUI automation, wall-clock time, token cost, and number of environment steps are critical. A method that doubles success rate but increases latency or cost by an order of magnitude may or may not be preferable depending on the application. Since the paper positions Agent S as a practical framework, some measurement of average steps, tokens, latency, or cost per successful task would be very helpful.

There are also some presentation issues. The writing is often understandable, but the prose is overly passive and sometimes awkward, which obscures the technical content. Several claims could be stated more precisely. There are also citation and editing issues: for example, the references contain what appears to be a duplicated AutoGuide entry under 2024a/2024b with identical metadata, and some benchmark/model references seem mismatched or imprecise. The mathematical presentation in Section 3.1.1 is also oddly formatted and could be cleaned up. These are not fatal issues, but they detract from polish.

On the technical side, I would have liked a deeper analysis of why the ACI helps. Is the main benefit better grounding, reduced action entropy, or better temporal abstraction? The error analysis suggests grounding and execution remain dominant failure modes, so it would be useful to quantify how often the accessibility tree alone suffices, how much OCR adds beyond the tree, and whether the bounded action space ever prevents necessary fine-grained interactions. Similarly, the hierarchical planner is claimed to help long-horizon tasks, but the evidence is indirect. A breakdown by task horizon or number of required app transitions would make this claim more convincing.

The WindowsAgentArena results are encouraging but should be interpreted cautiously. The overall gain from 13.3% to 18.2% is meaningful, but category performance is mixed, with Agent S underperforming NAVI on web browser and media/video tasks and tying at 0% on Office. Since the benchmark is contemporaneous and the comparison is to a “similar configuration” rather than necessarily the strongest accessible baseline, the generalization claim should be toned down somewhat. It shows transfer potential, but not yet broad dominance across operating systems.

In terms of significance, I think the paper is valuable because GUI agents are an important frontier and strong open implementations are scarce. The code release is a major plus. If the reported gains are reproducible, Agent S could become a useful reference framework for future work. However, for a top-tier ML venue, I would want stronger evidence disentangling the contributions, clearer handling of memory contamination and online adaptation, and more rigorous reporting of variance and efficiency.

My main suggestions for improvement are as follows. First, clarify the evaluation protocol around memory construction and continual updates: specify exactly what data are used before test time, whether memory is reset between tasks, whether task order is fixed, and whether any benchmark-derived environments are used in exploration. Second, add more controlled comparisons on the full benchmark, especially with and without web search, with and without ACI, and with frozen versus continually updated memory. Third, report efficiency metrics such as average steps, wall-clock time, and approximate API/token cost. Fourth, provide some measure of statistical uncertainty. Fifth, deepen the analysis of memory quality and retrieval relevance, perhaps with examples of helpful and harmful retrieved experiences. Sixth, improve the writing and tighten claims of novelty.

My overall assessment is positive but not unreservedly so. The paper presents a strong practical system with substantial empirical gains on a hard benchmark, and the architecture is sensible and likely useful to the community. The main limitations are that the novelty is somewhat incremental at the component level, and the evaluation leaves important questions about fairness, contamination, and efficiency unanswered. If those concerns are addressed, this could be a strong contribution.

I would lean toward a weak accept or borderline accept, depending on the venue’s emphasis. For a conference that values impactful empirical systems work and open-source agent frameworks, the paper is compelling. For a venue prioritizing crisp algorithmic novelty and airtight experimental isolation, it is less convincing in its current form.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper presents Agent S, an open framework for autonomous GUI-based computer control using multimodal LLMs. The system combines three main ideas: (1) experience-augmented hierarchical planning, where a manager decomposes tasks into subtasks using online web search and retrieved narrative memory; (2) worker-level execution with episodic memory retrieval and trajectory reflection; and (3) an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) that combines screenshots with an augmented accessibility tree and constrains actions to language-level GUI primitives. Experiments on OSWorld report an improvement from 11.21% to 20.58% success rate over a GPT-4o baseline, with additional gains on WindowsAgentArena. The paper also includes ablations on memory, web knowledge, hierarchical planning, and ACI, plus qualitative examples and error analysis.
strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: general-purpose GUI agents for desktop environments.
The overall framework is well-motivated and modular, combining planning, memory, retrieval, and interface design in a coherent architecture.
The ACI design is practically meaningful: accessibility-tree grounding plus bounded primitive actions is a sensible abstraction for GUI control.
Empirical gains on OSWorld are substantial in absolute terms relative to the reported baseline, and the paper evaluates on the full benchmark rather than only a tiny subset.
Ablation studies attempt to isolate the contributions of web knowledge, narrative memory, episodic memory, hierarchical planning, and ACI.
Cross-benchmark evaluation on WindowsAgentArena strengthens the claim that the approach is not narrowly overfit to one environment.
The paper includes useful qualitative discussion and error categorization, which helps diagnose remaining bottlenecks.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: many ingredients—hierarchical planning, retrieval-augmented prompting, episodic/narrative memory, reflection, accessibility-tree grounding, and constrained action spaces—have appeared in prior agent literature, and the main contribution is largely integration.
The empirical performance, while improved, remains low in absolute terms (20.58% on OSWorld), limiting the practical significance of the claimed human-like computer use.
The paper lacks rigorous statistical treatment: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run variance are reported despite likely high stochasticity in LLM-agent evaluation.
The memory construction and continual update protocol raises concerns about benchmark contamination and evaluation fairness, especially because memory is updated during inference on benchmark tasks.

The self-supervised exploration tasks are derived from applications and initial environments from OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena, which may leak benchmark-specific structure and reduce the strength of generalization claims.
Several important implementation details are underspecified, including retrieval corpus size, memory growth control, prompt formats, replanning frequency, step budgets, and cost/runtime overhead.

Comparison baselines are not always maximally fair or strongest available; some comparisons use different action abstractions or inaccessible proprietary systems, making attribution of gains less clean.

The paper makes strong claims about continual learning and self-improvement, but evidence is limited to benchmark-level performance rather than controlled longitudinal evaluation on non-overlapping task distributions.
methodological_flaws: The most serious methodological issue is potential evaluation leakage: the agent performs continual memory updates during inference, and initial memory is bootstrapped using tasks generated from benchmark applications and even benchmark initial environments. This blurs the line between training/exploration and test evaluation, making the reported success rates difficult to interpret as clean zero-shot generalization.

The claim that the self-evaluator assesses success/failure 'without any human feedback or ground truth information' is scientifically weak unless the exact criteria are specified and validated. If success labels are noisy or based on the agent's own judgment, memory updates may reinforce incorrect behaviors; the paper does not quantify evaluator accuracy.

The mathematical formalization is superficial and in places inconsistent. For example, the fusion equations are not really equations but a procedural table, and K_fused is written as LLM(M_n(Q), K_web) after already defining E_{n_u} as the retrieved memory item, suggesting notation sloppiness. There is no formal objective, no proof of correctness, and no analysis of retrieval/planning error propagation.

The ablation methodology is limited by a small sampled subset of 65 tasks, with no variance estimates. Given the stochasticity of MLLM agents, differences such as 20.00% vs 26.15% may not be statistically reliable.

The comparison between Agent S and baselines may confound architectural improvements with interface/action-space changes. Since ACI changes both observation representation and action abstraction, gains cannot be cleanly attributed to planning/memory alone.

The generalization claim to WindowsAgentArena is weakened by the fact that initial exploration also uses tasks from WindowsAgentArena applications/environments, so the evaluation is not a strict no-adaptation transfer setting.

The paper does not report computational cost, latency, or number of environment steps, despite introducing web search, retrieval, hierarchical planning, reflection, and memory updates. This omission is important because improved success may come at impractical cost.

Error analysis is descriptive but not methodologically rigorous: categories are overlapping, annotation protocol is unspecified, and no inter-rater reliability or reproducibility details are provided.
